items.title: Maritime CEO Forum: Dry bulk owners eye generational rate rally
items.original_title: Maritime CEO Forum: Dry bulk owners eye generational rate rally
items.summary: Dry bulk shipping could be approaching a generational freight rate rally as surging West African mineral exports transform tonne-mile demand, according to shipowners speaking at last week’s Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco, although concerns remain over the rapid expansion of Chinese shipbuilding capacity. John Michael Radziwill, chairman of CTM, argued that 2026 had exceeded expectations and that geopolitical disruption was proving supportive of freight markets. “I think we’re probably on the cusp of a generational rate rally,” he told the session, moderated by Mandarin Shipping chairman Tim Huxley, pointing out that dry bulk had yet to experience the extraordinary earnings witnessed in other shipping sectors since 2021. At Geneva Dry six months ago, expectations were for Simandou exports of 45m tonnes next year. The dry bulk orderbook remains relatively manageable at around 16% of the existing fleet, rising to approximately 19% for capesizes, according to Pappas. Pappas cited modern kamsarmax sales at $44m to $45m and capesize resales exceeding $90m. D’Amico questioned the economics of paying $46m for a 66,000 dwt ultramax, calculating that it would need to earn more than $18,000 daily over 20 years. Asked where they would invest today, d’Amico favoured people and operational improvements over additional ships, while Radziwill revealed CTM had acquired 12 vessels since May.

items.title: Muscat charts maritime resilience framework
items.original_title: Muscat charts maritime resilience framework
items.summary: Asyad Group, the end-to-end logistics solutions flagship of the Sultanate of Oman, is seeking to develop what it describes as the world’s first fully integrated maritime resilience framework, bringing international industry leaders together to establish practical priorities for safeguarding supply chains and sustaining global trade amid mounting operational and commercial pressures. The proposed Muscat Maritime Resilience Framework is the central initiative of the Muscat Maritime Resilience Forum 2026, which opened on Tuesday with discussions on strengthening maritime networks, improving preparedness and translating industry experience into coordinated action. The commercial stakes were highlighted by an Asyad operational study showing a 137 per cent variation in the total cost of a maritime voyage between India and Suhar. Speaking at the opening, Asyad Group Chief Executive Abdulrahman bin Salim al Hatmi said the framework would draw on the expertise of maritime leaders and practitioners to address challenges affecting costs, business continuity and commercial operations. “For the first time, international maritime leaders and practitioners are coming together in Muscat to contribute to the development of what we intend to be the world’s first-ever, fully integrated maritime resilience framework,” he said.

items.title: Offshore Industry Sends Urgent Call To EU Policymakers For Fit-For-Purpose EU ETS And MRV Framework
items.original_title: Offshore Industry Sends Urgent Call To EU Policymakers For Fit-For-Purpose EU ETS And MRV Framework
items.summary: Eight maritime associations including the Royal Belgian Shipowners’ Association (KBRV) send an open letter to EU policymakers urging them to ensure a fit-for-purpose framework for the European offshore sector under the current EU ETS review. The offshore shipping sector is a strategic asset to the European economy, playing a leading role in the continent’s energy transition, energy security and industrial competitiveness. Yet the current EU ETS framework, entering into force beginning 2027 for offshore vessels, will distort competition and create opportunities for circumvention, based on a Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) framework that was not designed for offshore operations and is widely recognised as not fit for purpose. The sector strongly urges EU policymakers to first ensure that a fit-for purpose activity-based MRV framework is operational, before the inclusion of offshore vessels above 5000GT in EU ETS from next year onwards. Below is the open letter the sector has addressed to the European Parliament and members of the Council EU ETS REVIEW: GET THE FRAMEWORK RIGHT FOR EUROPE’S OFFSHORE SECTOR Open letter to Members of the European Parliament and EU Member States’ Permanent Representatives.

items.title: LNG Carrier Prices Fall to $245 Million, Threatening Korean Shipbuilders’ Margins
items.original_title: LNG Carrier Prices Fall to $245 Million, Threatening Korean Shipbuilders’ Margins
items.summary: Prices for high-value vessels, including liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers and ultra-large container ships, have begun to decline despite rising demand. Intensifying competition from Chinese shipbuilders entering the premium vessel market, coupled with their aggressive supply strategies, is putting downward pressure on newbuilding prices. According to UK-based shipping market intelligence provider Clarksons Research, the benchmark newbuilding price for an LNG carrier stood at $245 million as of Oct. Prices for ultra-large container ships also declined over the same period, from $266.5 million to approximately $242 million. The downturn is particularly notable given that LNG carrier orders have increased more than 4.5-fold year-on-year. Jiangnan Shipyard has also intensified price competition by securing LNG carrier orders at $225 million per vessel, undercutting prevailing benchmark prices and challenging South Korean shipbuilders’ market share. South Korean shipbuilders are unlikely to experience an immediate earnings impact, as this year’s results largely reflect vessels ordered at peak prices approximately two years ago. With shipping capacity expanding ahead of available cargo volumes, shipowners have less incentive to pay premium prices for new vessels. Industry experts say South Korean shipbuilders need to accelerate technological development and business diversification to maintain their competitive edge over Chinese rivals.

Both need to move cargo across international waters and into a port without the voyage being reconstructed afterward. Going dark at the point where the record would matter. Sanctioned operators use it to break the link between cargo and origin. Trafficking networks use it for the same structural reason. The limits are worth stating honestly: A high-speed craft operating at up to 40 knots can be outside the frame by the time imagery is processed and delivered, which is why detection at the mothership end of the chain is more tractable than at the receiving end. Screened against ownership networks and multi-year behavioral history, the underlying identity remains traceable. The Mali-flagged vessel above had reflagged in June 2026 following a renaming and a series of identity changes. Asia remained firm amid lighter trading with the North still the driving force with a 63,000-dwt ex dry dock China fixed to West Africa with generals at $28,000, whilst the South Pacific was more subdued this week. items.title: US suspends Chinese vessel port fees for 2 months, will accept public comment
items.original_title: US suspends Chinese vessel port fees for 2 months, will accept public comment
items.summary: The US Trade Representative (USTR) will take public comment through 30 October and is suspending the implementation of port fees for Chinese vessels by two months as officials from both countries continue to negotiate broader trade issues. The new fees were set to take effect on 10 November after the US and China agreed in November 2025 to suspend tit-for-tat maritime charges for one year as part of a broader trade agreement. They will now take effect on 9 January if no other agreement is reached. The temporary suspension means that no parties will accrue liability for, or be required to pay, the transport service fees or associated product duties during the extended window. The US initially targeted the fees for ships owned, operated, or built in China in October 2025, prompting China to enact similar charges for US-linked ships entering Chinese ports. The initial USTR proposal was published in February 2025 in the Federal Register and included proposed service fees of up to $1.5 million per US port call for vessels built in China, and up to $1 million per port call for China-based operators. The action was taken after a Section 301 investigation determined China’s acts, policies and practices to be unreasonable and to burden or restrict US commerce.

items.title: WinGD grows Korea engine production capacity with first HD Hyundai Marine Engine license
items.original_title: WinGD grows Korea engine production capacity with first HD Hyundai Marine Engine license
items.summary: Swiss marine power company WinGD has signed its first-ever license agreement with engine builder HD Hyundai Marine Engine (formerly STX Heavy Industries). The agreement will significantly extend WinGD’s capability to deliver its dual-fuel and diesel engine designs to bulk carrier and tanker newbuild projects in Korea and other markets using Korea-built two-stroke engines. HD Hyundai Marine Engine was acquired by HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering, part of HD Hyundai Group, in 2024. Its expertise in small and mid-sized two-stroke engines complements the large engine specialism of HD Hyundai Heavy Industries, with which WinGD has a long-standing license agreement, and which delivers engines for large vessels including ultra-large container vessels and LNG carriers. WinGD Vice President Product Centre, Peter Krähenbühl was on hand for the signing and said: “This new agreement expands our ability to deliver main engines for high-volume vessel segments in Korea and enables HD Hyundai Marine Engine’s customers to select WinGD engine technology. We look forward to working closely with HD Hyundai Marine Engine to strengthen the availability and competitiveness of WinGD’s mid-bore engine portfolio .” Under the agreement, WinGD and HD Hyundai Marine Engine will share knowledge and experience to continue reducing the cost and improving vessel design integration of WinGD’s mid-bore engines, while safeguarding their high reliability and in-service performance.

items.title: Can carriers avoid overcapacity in 2027?
items.original_title: Can carriers avoid overcapacity in 2027?
items.summary: The backdrop is difficult to ignore. Around 5 mteu of new capacity has been ordered in each of the past three years, pushing the orderbook-to-fleet ratio to approximately 45%, its highest level since 2009. The orderbook is fast approaching 16 mteu, with September the second-busiest contracting month on record at 1.1 mteu, following major orders from the world’s two largest carriers: MSC (20 × 24,000 teu) and Maersk (20 × 18,600 teu). Ultimately, the 2027 outcome will depend on whether demand growth, slow steaming and congestion can absorb capacity faster than new ships enter service. Overcapacity is, in our view, unavoidable. More than 70% expect some degree of overcapacity in 2027, with 56.7% anticipating a moderate surplus and 14.2% predicting significant overcapacity. Blank sailings, service adjustments and other measures can help contain the surplus, but respondents appear unconvinced that carriers can fully offset the delivery pipeline. Cargo demand attracted just 11.7%, while demolitions accounted for only 1.3%, suggesting that neither stronger demand nor the removal of older tonnage is widely expected to be the decisive factor. Our view The poll reinforces our assessment that 2027 will be a test of carriers’ ability to manage a growing capacity surplus rather than prevent one altogether.

items.summary: MacGregor has received an order of PLC (Programmable Logic Controller) retrofit projects for 35 Pure Car and Truck Carrier (PCTC) vessels for Wallenius Wilhelmsen. The order was booked into MacGregor’s third quarter 2026 order intake, and the upgrades will take place based on the vessels’ sailing schedule and availability. Securing this contract highlights MacGregor’s deep technical expertise and strong relationship with Wallenius Wilhelmsen. The scope of supply for the 35 vessels includes PLC upgrade of the ships’ quarter ramps. In line with Wallenius Wilhelmsen’s sustainability targets, the replaced PLCs will be stored onboard as spare parts for remaining RoRo equipment onboard or other vessels with the same equipment. “Facing a tight market and high customer expectations, Wallenius Wilhelmsen is focused on reducing operational disruptions while delivering high-end service and uncompromised reliability to our customers. items.title: Shipping Strikes In Hormuz Leave Both Sides With Economic Pain
items.original_title: Shipping Strikes In Hormuz Leave Both Sides With Economic Pain
items.summary: Smoke and fire rise from a commercial cargo vessel following a strike, which US Central Command says it had disabled in the Gulf of Oman after the ship's crew ignored warnings and attempted to run a naval blockade against Iran, at a location given as the Gulf of Oman, October 10, 2026, in this still image taken from a handout video. U.S. Central Command/Handout via REUTERS Oct 31, 2026 (Bloomberg) –As US President Donald Trump threatens renewed attacks against Iran, Tehran’s intermittent strikes on commercial vessels have left the two sides locked in a painful economic standoff. And for the US, the rising cost of shipping oil through the Strait of Hormuz — even though US Central Command says almost all Iranian attacks there fail or are intercepted — has kept fuel prices high, stirring a political backlash at home with the midterm elections fast approaching. But even significant economic pain isn’t likely to change Iran’s ability to keep up “ harassing fire ” in the strait, said Jim Lamson, a visiting research fellow in the Department of War Studies at King’s College London and former CIA analyst focused on Iran and the Middle East.

items.title: Taiwan Says China Harassing Shipping With East Coast Patrol
items.original_title: Taiwan Says China Harassing Shipping With East Coast Patrol
items.summary: A Taiwan Coast Guard patrol vessel moves in Keelung, as China conducts "Justice Mission 2025" military drills around Taiwan, in Keelung, Taiwan, December 30, 2025. REUTERS/Ann Wang TAIPEI, Nov 1 (Reuters) – China’s Coast Guard is harassing shipping with its latest patrol off Taiwan’s east coast and trying to exert a fictional jurisdiction, the Taiwanese Coast Guard said, adding it had sent its own ships to keep watch. China, which views Taiwan as its own territory, has stepped up activity off the island’s east coast since June with regular coast guard patrols. Taiwan’s Coast Guard said China’s “attempts to harass ships at sea through radio communications are a clear expansion of power that violate international law, undermine regional peace and stability, and deviate from reality.” “Our country holds sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the exclusive economic zone east of Taiwan, and China has absolutely no jurisdiction over any of Taiwan’s waters,” it added. China on Saturday also sent another Coast Guard ship close to the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands, which are strategically located at the top of the South China Sea, Taiwan’s Coast Guard said separately. Taiwan has so far this year “expelled” Chinese Coast Guard vessels from Pratas waters 13 times, it added.
